title: Buying Gold Coins in Los Angeles: Coin Shop vs. Pure
summary: Buying gold coins in Los Angeles? Local coin shop vs. Pure's order book on authentication, bid and ask, fees, delivery, order finality, and California tax.
body_markdown:
If you want to buy gold coins in Los Angeles and you are open to buying online, Pure answers the two questions that matter most: **the spread is on the screen before you commit, and the coin is tested before it ships to you.** A local coin shop is the better fit when you want the coin in your hand today, want to pay cash, or already trust the person behind the counter. Plenty of buyers use both, and this comparison is about matching the path to the purchase in front of you.


We run Pure, so read the verdict with that in mind. Everything below about the shop side is written as what to ask, because shops differ and we are not going to tell you what any particular counter in the city does.


## The coin shop path


You walk in, maybe somewhere in the downtown Jewelry District, maybe a neighborhood coin store, look at what is in the case, get a price, and pay. If the shop tests metal, you can watch it happen. You can hold the coin, compare two dates side by side, find out what the dealer would pay to buy it back, and leave with it in your pocket. The tradeoffs: selection is whatever is in the case that day, terms differ from one shop to the next, and the checks are only as good as the questions you remember to ask.


## The Pure path


Collect Pure is a peer-to-peer marketplace for gold, silver, platinum, and palladium coins and bars, plus rare coins. Two collectors founded it in 2022, one a former professional numismatist. It is a Y Combinator company from the Summer 2023 batch. Buyers and sellers post their own prices. Each product page shows the highest bid and lowest ask, every order is visible, and you can accept the lowest ask to buy immediately or place a bid at your own price. On a standard marketplace order, the seller ships to Pure first, the item is tested in house, and then it ships to you. The tradeoff is time: about a day for verification once the item arrives, then transit to you. More in[how the Pure marketplace works](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/how-the-pure-marketplace-works) .

## Authentication is the first question


Gold's counterfeit problem is specific. Tungsten is close enough to gold in density that a correctly sized fake passes a scale, so a weight-and-dimensions check is only a first pass and a composition or conductivity test matters. At a shop, find out what tool they use, whether they will run it on the coin you are buying while you stand there, and whether the result goes on the receipt.


On Pure the test is part of the process, and it happens on every item before the buyer ever handles it. The seller ships to Pure. We test the metal's exact composition, the unboxing and inspection are recorded on camera, and a trained specialist checks each item by hand. Items that clear are labeled Pure Qualified. For a slabbed coin you can also run the cert number through[NGC's lookup](https://www.ngccoin.com/certlookup/) or PCGS's equivalent yourself, from the listing, before you bid.


## Seeing the bid and the ask before money moves


At a shop, the price on the tag is one side of a two-sided market. The other side is what the dealer would pay you for that coin. If only one is on the tag, ask for the other. The gap between them is the spread, and it tells you more about the price than the tag alone does. Check either number against the[LBMA gold price](https://www.lbma.org.uk/prices-and-data/lbma-gold-price) and you have the premium in dollars as well.


On Pure, the two numbers are the page. The highest bid and the lowest ask sit next to each other, and the order book below them shows what other buyers and sellers have posted. Each listing also shows its premium over the live spot price, so the subtraction is already done. The ask is what you pay if you want the coin now. The bid is where you post your own price and wait. Pick any coin on the[marketplace](https://www.collectpure.com/marketplace) and both are there; if reading one is new to you, the[beginner's guide to reading an order book](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/how-to-read-an-order-book-beginners-guide) walks through a listing line by line.


## Fees, payment, and what a card costs you


Two payment questions for any shop: is there a card surcharge, and is there a different price for cash. The answers vary; get them before the total is rung up.


Pure charges buyers no marketplace fee. Bank wire and ACH work on every order. Cards are accepted only on Pure Priority orders, Pure's daily drop section, and carry a 2.9% surcharge, so a $5,000 Pure Priority purchase on a card costs $145 more than the same purchase by wire. Shipping is $25 on orders under $10,000 and free above that. On a $2,600 coin that $25 is about 1% of the price. On a $500 fractional coin it is 5%, which is one reason small purchases are where a local counter can make more sense.


## Shipping, insurance, and order finality


A shop hands you the coin and from that moment it is yours, including the drive home.


Pure ships every item insured both ways, up to $125,000. Check-in takes about a day after the seller's package lands, and the coin ships to you once it clears, with the test at the front of that.


Finality is where the two paths feel most different. A shop's return window, if it offers one, is something to get in writing, along with how the price is treated if spot moves before you bring the coin back. On Pure, your price locks when the order is confirmed, and confirmed buy orders cannot be cancelled by the buyer. That is stricter than a return window, and it is not the whole of the terms: if an item fails the check, Pure tries to fill your order from another seller at the same price, and refunds you in full if it cannot. The reason it works is sequencing: the question a return policy exists to answer, whether the coin is real and as described, gets settled by the in-house check before the item ever reaches you.


## Who each path suits


The shop fits the buyer who wants the coin today, wants to pay cash, wants to compare two dates in hand, or has a dealer they have bought from for years. It also fits small purchases, where $25 of shipping is a real share of the total.


Pure fits the buyer who wants the spread on the screen before committing and the metal tested before the coin ships, who is buying at a size where shipping is a rounding error, and who is fine waiting out the test for a coin that has been checked by a person before it ships. That describes a lot of first-time buyers who already buy everything else online.


## California sales tax on gold coins


California treats bullion and coins differently depending on the size of the purchase. Under[CDTFA Regulation 1599](https://www.cdtfa.ca.gov/lawguides/vol1/sutr/1599.html) , sales of monetized bullion, nonmonetized gold or silver bullion, and numismatic coins are exempt from sales and use tax when the total market value in a single transaction is $2,000 or more (the threshold in effect since July 1, 2023) and the sale is made by or through a seller registered under the Commodity Exchange Act or not required to register. Below that amount the purchase is generally taxable. Rules change and your invoice is the final word, so confirm the treatment of your specific order before you buy.


## Questions about buying on Pure


### Can I see the coin before I pay on Pure?


Not in hand. You see the listing, and after the seller ships the item to Pure it is checked by a person before it goes to you. If handling the coin first is the deciding factor, the shop wins that one outright.


### Can I pay for gold coins with a credit card on Pure?


Only on Pure Priority orders, the daily drop section, and those carry a 2.9% surcharge. Every other order is bank wire or ACH.


### Can I cancel a buy order on Pure after it is confirmed?


No. The price locks at confirmation and confirmed buy orders cannot be cancelled by the buyer.
